sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Bunjil** ​(*bunjil*) — ‌Creator Eaglehawk ‌— belongs ​to the ​Aboriginal traditions ​of the ​Kulin nations ​in central ‌Victoria, Australia. ​The ​name means ‌'the eaglehawk' ​and refers ‌to the ​wedge-tailed eagle ‌ancestor who ​shaped Country, ​gave law, ​and then ​withdrew ​into the ‌sky.

In ​Kulin cosmology ‌Bunjil is ​one of ‌two moiety ​ancestors, paired ‌with Waang ​the ‌crow. The ​stories credit ​him with ‌forming the ‌land's surface, ‌establishing social ​and ecological ​obligations, and ‌finally ascending ​to ​become the ‌star Altair. ​His wives ​became the ‌black swans ​beside him, ‌and his ​son Binbeal ​is the ​rainbow.

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Bunjil**. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*bunjil* is ​a technological ‌compromise required ‌by the ‌domain-name ‌system: it ​drops only ‌the capital ​initial that ​marks a ​proper name ‌in English ​scholarly citation. ​Because ​the Kulin ‌languages were ​traditionally oral ​and the ​ASCII spelling ‌already contains ​the conventional ‌transcription, the ​restoration is ‌classified ​as Tier ‌2. The ‌Unicode form ​remains the ​scholarly reference; ​the ASCII ​form is ‌a practical ‌convenience for ​DNS.

Massola, Aldo. Bunjil's Cave: Myths, Legends and Superstitions of the Aborigines of South-East Australia (Lansdowne Press, 1968).
Mudrooroo. Aboriginal Mythology: An A–Z (Thorsons, 1994).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​**Bunjil** is a theonym ‌recorded from the ‌Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, and related ​Kulin languages of ​central Victoria. It ​denotes the wedge-tailed eaglehawk ​as creator ancestor. ​Because these languages were ‌— and in ​revitalisation efforts continue to ​be — oral ‌traditions, there is no ​pre-colonial alphabetic original ‌script. The name ​survives in Latin transcriptions ‌made by early ​settlers, missionaries, and anthropologists.

​The PuniCodex restoration ​**Bunjil** simply supplies the ​capital initial that ​English and Australian scholarly ‌convention uses for ​a proper name. ‌The ASCII form *bunjil* ​is therefore not ‌an ancient spelling; it ​is a DNS ‌compromise that flattens the ​name into all-lowercase ‌letters. The spoken name ​and the mythic ​role remain intact.

‌The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

‌- **b** → ‌**B** — capitalised as ​a proper name
​- **u** → **u** ‌— same
- ​**n** → **n** — ​same
- **j** ‌→ **j** — ​same
- **i** → ​**i** — same
‌- **l** → **l** ​— same

No ‌distinctive diacritic or special ​letter is added, ​so the name ​remains Tier 2 in ​the PuniCodex system.

‌### Etymology

The name ‌**Bunjil** is attested ​as a theonym in ‌the Kulin languages ​of central Victoria, particularly ​Woiwurrung and Boonwurrung. ‌It refers to ‌the wedge-tailed eaglehawk (*Aquila ‌audax*) in its ‌ancestral, creative aspect. No ​reconstructed Proto-Pama–Nyungan form ‌can be offered with ​confidence; the word ​is recorded from the ​specific languages in ‌which Bunjil's cult ​was central.

Early colonial ​collectors produced a ​range of spellings — ‌Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, ​Bunjel, Punjel — as ​they attempted to ​write Aboriginal sounds with ‌English letters. Modern ​Kulin communities and ‌Victorian institutions generally prefer ​**Bunjil** or **Bundjil**.

‌Because the source languages ​were oral, the ‌'original script' question does ‌not arise in ​the usual sense. PuniCodex ​treats the capitalised ​Latin transcription **Bunjil** ​as the scholarly citation ‌form and the ‌lowercase **bunjil** as the ​DNS compromise.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional ​scholarly reading of the ‌name is **/ˈbʊn.dʒɪl/** ‌— English transcription ​of the Kulin theonym.

​For the modern ​speaker, the closest ​approximation is: **'BUN-jil'** — ​stress the first ‌syllable, pronounce the ​'j' as in 'jump', ​and keep the ‌final vowel short like ​the 'i' in ‌'kit'.

Because the ​ASCII form *bunjil* already ‌encodes the same ​conventional spelling, the ​restoration **Bunjil** does not ​add a stress ​mark, length mark, ​or distinctive letter. The ‌name is Tier ​2: the Unicode form ‌is the preferred ​scholarly citation, while ‌the ASCII form is ​the domain-name compromise.

‌Because Bunjil belongs ​to an oral tradition, ‌the reconstructed pronunciation ​offered here is ​a scholarly romanization rather ‌than a phonetic ‌record of a living ‌speaker. The sounds ​of the original ​language include phonemes that ‌English does not ​distinguish, and early ​recorders used inconsistent English-based ‌spellings. PuniCodex therefore ​treats the capitalized ​scholarly form **Bunjil** as ‌the reference spelling, ​while noting that the ‌ASCII form represents ​the same romanized ​sequence. This is why ​the name is ​classified as Tier ‌2: the restoration recovers ‌the proper-noun convention ​of the name ‌without adding a diacritic ​or special letter ​that the original ASCII ‌string could not ‌carry.

sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous writing ‌system ‌is securely ​attested ​for ​individual aboriginal ​names. ​The form ‌shown ​is a ​modern ‌scholarly transliteration.[^1]

​The ‌form ​**Bunjil** is ‌therefore ​a scholarly ​transliteration ​rather than ​an ​attested ancient ‌spelling; ​it ‌encodes the ​reconstructed ‌sound of ​the ‌name for ​modern ‌use, and ​no ​mark ‌in it ‌is ‌decorative.

The ​Kulin ​languages were ‌traditionally ​oral, and ​Bunjil ‌has ​no original ​alphabetic ‌script. The ​name ‌survives in ​Latin ​transcription ​made by ​early ‌settlers and ‌anthropologists. ​PuniCodex therefore ‌treats ​**Bunjil** as ​the ‌scholarly ‌citation form ‌and ‌**bunjil** as ​the ‌DNS compromise. ​The ​restoration adds ​only ‌the ​capital initial; ​the ​absence of ‌diacritics ​or special ​letters ​places the ‌name ​in ‌Tier 2, ​not ‌because the ​figure ‌is less ‌significant, ​but because ​the ​ASCII ​form already ‌carries ‌the conventional ​spelling.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Bunjil's ​domain is ‌creation itself, ‌conceived ​not as ​a ​single moment ​but as ​an ‌ongoing relationship ​with Country. ​In ‌Kulin thought ​he ‌is the ​wedge-tailed eaglehawk ‌who ​shaped the ​physical world, ​established ​law, and ​then ‌took his ​place in ‌the ​sky as ‌a continuing ​watcher.

‌His influence ​extends ‌across several ​registers. As ​**Creator ‌of Country** ‌he is ‌responsible ​for landforms, ​water, ‌plants, and ​animals. As ​**Law-Giver** ‌he established ​the obligations ​that ‌bind people ​to ‌one another ​and to ​the ​land. As ​**Sky Ancestor** ‌he ‌provides a ​celestial ‌point of ​reference, identified ​with ‌the star ‌Altair. As ‌**Moiety ‌Founder** he ​heads ‌the eaglehawk ​half of ​the ​Kulin social ‌order, balanced ​by ​Waang the ​crow.

‌These domains ​are not ​abstract ​categories; they ‌are lived ​in ‌the seasonal ​calendar, ‌the songlines, ​the rock-art ‌site ‌of Bunjil's ​Shelter, and ​the ​contemporary cultural ​and ‌environmental work ‌of Kulin ​communities.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Bunjil's stories belong ​to the Dreaming of ‌the Kulin nations, especially ‌the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, and ​Wathaurong peoples. They explain ​how Country was made, ​how law was given, ​and how the creator ​withdrew into the sky ‌so that he might ​continue to watch over ​the world.[^1]

### Shaping the ‌Land and the Law ​(Creation)

In the Dreaming, ‌Bunjil travelled across what ​is now central Victoria. ‌He formed the mountains, ​traced the rivers, named ​the plants and animals, ​and laid down the ​laws that govern how ​people relate to one ‌another and to Country. These ​laws are not separate ‌from the land; they ​are remembered in place ‌names, songlines, and the ​seasonal responsibilities of each ‌clan. (Massola 1968; Howitt ​1904)[^2]

### The Sea ‌That Would Not Stop ​Rising (Deluge)

A Boonwurrung ​story tells of a ‌time when the Kulin nations ‌fell into conflict, neglecting ‌family and Country. The ​sea rose in anger ​and threatened to flood ‌the land. The people ​went to Bunjil and ​asked him to intervene. ‌Bunjil agreed, but only ​if the people would ​change their ways and ‌respect the law. He walked ​to the water's edge, ‌raised his spear, and ​commanded the sea to ​stop. It did. (Briggs, ​'Boon Wurrung Story')

### ​Lifted into the Sky ‌(Ascent)

When his work ‌on earth was finished, ​Bunjil gathered his family ‌and asked Waang, who ​kept the winds in skin ​bags, to release enough ‌wind to carry them ‌to the sky. Waang ‌opened the whirlwind bag, ‌and the wind lifted ​Bunjil and his people ‌upward. Bunjil became the ​bright star Altair; his ​two wives, the black ​swans, became the stars ‌on either side. Some accounts ​say he left this ​world from the island ​of Deen Maar. (Howitt ‌1904; Mudrooroo 1994)

### ​Bunjil's Shelter (Sacred site)

​In Gariwerd, the country ​now known as the ‌Grampians, Bunjil took shelter ​in a cave in ‌the Black Range. The ​rock-art site known as Bunjil's ‌Shelter is one of ​the most important Aboriginal ‌art places in Victoria ‌and remains under the ​care of Traditional Owners. ​It is not merely ​a memory of the ​ancestor; it is a ‌place where his presence ‌is understood to remain. ​(Parks Victoria 2009)

Mudrooroo. Aboriginal Mythology: An A–Z (Thorsons, 1994).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Bunjil ​is not ‌a ‌solitary deity ​but ​one ​half of ​a ​Kulin social ‌and ​cosmological pair. ​The ‌eaglehawk moiety, ​headed ‌by ​Bunjil, is ‌balanced ​by the ​crow ​moiety, headed ​by ​Waang. This ‌pairing ​structures ‌kinship, marriage, ​and ‌ritual obligations ​across ‌the Kulin ​nations. ‌Different clans ​emphasise ​different ‌episodes — ‌the ‌Woiwurrung stress ​the ​sky ascent ‌and ​Altair, the ​Boonwurrung ‌remember ​the rising-sea ​story, ‌and the ​Wathaurong ‌preserve place-based ​accounts ​tied ​to the ​coast ‌and to ‌Bunjil's ​Shelter. In ‌the ​colonial period ​the ‌name ‌was recorded ‌under ‌many spellings ​— ‌Winjeel, Wingeel, ​Pundjel, ​Bunjel — ​reflecting ‌dialect ​variation and ​the ​difficulty of ‌rendering ​Aboriginal phonology ​in ​English orthography.[^1]

‌Kindred ​figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition index ​include ‌[[ahuramazda|AhuraMazdā]], [[audhumla|Auðhumla]], ‌[[baiame|Baiame]], ​[[izanagi|Izanagi]], [[jagannatha|Jagannātha]], ​and ​[[oduduwa|Odùduwà]], ​each linked ‌through ‌creator / ​cosmogonic.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Bunjil ​teaches that ‌creation ‌is ​not a ​single ​event ​but a ​continuing ‌responsibility. ​He did ​not ‌make the ​land ‌and ​depart; he ‌shaped ​it, ​gave it ​law, ​and ​then withdrew ‌into ​the sky ‌so ​that ‌he could ​go ‌on ​watching. The ‌eaglehawk's ​eye ​is still ‌understood ‌to be ‌turned ​toward ​Country.

For ‌non-Indigenous ​visitors, ​Bunjil is ‌an ​invitation ​to understand ‌'Country' ​not as ‌real ​estate ​but as ​a ​living ‌inheritance — ‌a ​place ‌that includes ​people, ​animals, plants, ‌water, ‌sky, ‌and story, ‌all ​held ‌together by ​obligations ​that ​precede the ‌colony. ​The name ​Bunjil, ​even ‌in its ​simple ​Latin ​transcription, carries ‌that ​whole ‌relationship. To ​restore ‌the capital ​is ‌a ‌small act; ​to ​remember ​what it ​names ‌is ‌the larger ​one.[^1]
